idiom_name: ViewModelBase : INotifyPropertyChanged + RelayCommand : ICommand bound from XAML
implementation_notes: The .NET binding engine does the observing: the view-model implements INotifyPropertyChanged and raises PropertyChanged with the exact property name after each change, exposes commands as ICommand (the RelayCommand pattern from Josh Smith's WPF article), and the view binds to them in XAML with the view-model as DataContext. The docs warn that a wrong property-name string is a subtle runtime bug, so verify names in DEBUG; collections need ObservableCollection<T> because INotifyPropertyChanged does not cover them. This remains the portable baseline for WPF, MAUI, WinUI and Avalonia.
pitfalls: A PropertyChanged raised with the wrong (or stale) property name is a silent bug: the engine re-queries a property that did not change - verify names in DEBUG.
Raising PropertyChanged mid-operation exposes a half-updated object to bindings and can cascade; raise once, at the end, only when the value really changed.
INotifyPropertyChanged does not cover collections: bind to ObservableCollection<T> (INotifyCollectionChanged) or list changes never reach the view.
Two-way bindings write straight into the view-model; without IDataErrorInfo/INotifyDataErrorInfo or setter validation, invalid values reach the model.

variants.name: CommunityToolkit.Mvvm source-generated view-models
variants.implementation_notes: The .NET Community MVVM Toolkit generates the boilerplate at compile time: ObservableObject supplies PropertyChanged/PropertyChanging and SetProperty helpers, [ObservableProperty] turns a field into a notifying property, [RelayCommand] turns a method into an ICommand, and compiled bindings (x:Bind, or {Binding} where required) connect the view. Prefer it over hand-written setters for new .NET code; keep the classic form for legacy codebases and for targets where the generated code size or trimming behaviour matters.
pitfalls: Assigning the backing field directly bypasses the generated property and skips notifications; mutate through the generated property.
The generator requires a partial class and a C# 9+ compiler; mixing generated notifications with hand-written PropertyChanged handlers in one hierarchy double-notifies.
Compiled bindings (x:Bind, typical with [ObservableProperty]) default to OneTime: forgetting Mode=OneWay/TwoWay is a silent stale-UI bug.
